Every microphone turns air pressure into voltage, but the three main types do it differently, and that
changes how they sound, how loud a source they can take and how fragile they are.

## Dynamic

A thin diaphragm glued to a coil of wire, sitting in a magnet. Sound moves the coil, the magnet makes a
current. The Shure SM57 and SM58 are the classic examples.

- **Tough**: dropped, rained on, shouted into, they keep working.
- **Handles very loud sources**: snare, kick, guitar amps, brass close up.
- Less detail in the highs and less sensitive, so it picks up **less of the room** and less bleed. That is
  why it is the default for live sound and for recording in an untreated bedroom.
- Needs a lot of preamp gain (often 50–60 dB on a quiet voice). Some very low-output ones (the Shure
  SM7B) are used with an inline booster.
- **No phantom power needed.**

## Condenser

A very thin, electrically charged diaphragm close to a metal back plate: a capacitor whose value changes
as the diaphragm moves. It needs power to hold the charge and to run its small internal amplifier.

- **Detailed and sensitive**: the air on a voice, the pick on an acoustic guitar, cymbals, overheads, a
  piano, a choir or a room.
- **Large-diaphragm** (an inch or so; the studio vocal mic) sounds warm and flattering; **small-diaphragm**
  ("pencil" mics) is more accurate and even off-axis, good for acoustic instruments and stereo pairs.
- Picks up **everything**: the fridge, the computer fan, the reflections off the walls. In a bare room a
  condenser can sound worse than a dynamic.
- More fragile. Keep it out of the damp and away from kick drums unless it is built for it.
- **Needs phantom power** (or its own power supply, for valve/tube condensers).

## Ribbon

A strip of very thin corrugated aluminium hung in a magnetic field.

- Smooth, dark, natural highs; loved on guitar amps, brass, strings and drum rooms.
- Almost always **figure-8** (picks up front and back equally).
- **Fragile**: a blast of air (a kick drum, a puff into it, being carried quickly) can stretch the ribbon.
  Keep it covered when not in use.
- Classic passive ribbons do **not** want phantom power, and old ones can be damaged by a faulty cable
  with it on. Active ribbons (they say so) need it.

## Phantom power (+48 V)

Phantom power sends 48 volts DC down the same balanced XLR cable that brings the signal back. It is
"phantom" because a dynamic mic, wired the usual way, doesn't see it at all.

- Turn it on for **condensers** (and active ribbons, and some DI boxes).
- **Plug in first, then switch on.** Switch **off and wait** a few seconds before unplugging. Plugging in
  with 48 V live makes a loud pop through the speakers and can, rarely, harm gear.
- **Monitors down** when switching it on or off.
- On many cheap interfaces one 48 V button powers two or all inputs at once. Fine for dynamics; check
  before plugging an old ribbon into any of them.
- If a condenser makes no sound: is 48 V on? Is it an XLR cable (not a jack)?

<div class="sk-care">Never patch an XLR in or out with phantom power on, and keep vintage ribbon mics
on a channel with 48 V off.</div>

Try the order yourself. Press **Monitors on** (speakers low), choose a mic, then plug in and switch
+48 V in the right and the wrong order:

## Polar patterns

The **polar pattern** is how sensitive a mic is from each direction.

- **Cardioid** (heart-shaped): picks up the front, rejects the back. The default for almost everything.
  Point the back at what you *don't* want (the drums, the monitor, the window).
- **Supercardioid / hypercardioid**: narrower in front, with a small lobe at the back. Common on live
  vocal mics. Point the *side* (not the back) at the monitor.
- **Omni**: everything equally. Natural, no proximity effect (see [placement](rec-placement.qmd)), but
  hears the whole room.
- **Figure-8**: front and back, nothing from the sides. Ribbons; two singers facing each other; the side
  mic of a mid/side pair ([Sound 23: Stereo](sound-stereo.qmd)).

Many large-diaphragm condensers have a switch for several of these.

<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="polar-patterns"></div>

### Off axis

A pattern drawing is for the middle frequencies. Off to the side, a mic doesn't just get quieter: the
treble drops first, because a diaphragm stops hearing high sounds that arrive from the side. So a singer
who wanders off the mic sounds further away *and* duller.

<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="off-axis"></div>

Walk the singer round the mic and listen:

<div class="rk" data-w="offaxis"></div>

### Don't cup the mic

A cardioid is directional because of the **rear ports**, slots behind the capsule: sound reaching them
from behind arrives at the back of the diaphragm too, and cancels. Wrap a hand round the grille and the
ports are covered. The mic becomes almost omni, hears the wedge monitor it was meant to ignore, and
feeds back. The hollow of the hand also makes a little chamber: the voice goes boxy and honky, and the
sound engineer can't EQ it back. Hold the handle.

<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="cupping"></div>

Press **Cup the grille** to hear (and see) it:

<div class="rk" data-w="offaxis" data-set="pat=card,dia=hand,angle=160" data-title="Cupping: the back stops being quiet"></div>

## Which mic for what

No mic is flat on purpose. A handheld vocal dynamic trims the bass (you'll be close, and proximity effect
puts it back) and lifts 4–6 kHz, where words are clear; a studio condenser stays near flat.

<div class="gear-fig" data-fig="mic-response"></div>

| Source | First choice | Also good |
|---|---|---|
| Voice in an untreated room | Dynamic (SM58, SM7B) | Cardioid condenser, close, with a pop filter |
| Voice in a treated room | Large-diaphragm condenser | Ribbon for a dark, vintage sound |
| Acoustic guitar | Small-diaphragm condenser | Large-diaphragm, or a pair |
| Electric guitar amp | Dynamic (SM57) on the speaker | Ribbon, or both blended |
| Snare, toms | Dynamic | |
| Kick | Large dynamic (built for kick) | Condenser outside the drum |
| Overheads, room | Pair of condensers | Ribbons |
| Piano | Pair of condensers | |
| Bass, keys | DI | Mic on the bass amp as well |
